slides.title: Searching and Sorting
slides.main: Two problems are everywhere: finding what you need and putting data in order.

captions: Unordered data: until we scan it all, we can't know it's absent — O(n)
Ordered data: each step discards half — O(log n)
To search fast, order the data first — the second half of the lesson

slides.title: Binary search
slides.sub: Open the dictionary in the middle
slides.main: One comparison step removes half the book.

captions: Looking for 23 in a sorted array: two bounds and a midpoint
Middle 16 is smaller than the target — discard the left half
Middle 56 is larger — discard the right part
Three comparisons instead of six; for a million, about twenty

slides.title: Two hard requirements
slides.main: Sorted order plus constant-time access: a pair for a whole career.

captions: First: the data is ordered — otherwise we can't discard half
Second: the middle is reached in O(1), as in an array
In a linked list you follow links to the middle: all savings vanish

slides.title: Discipline of boundaries
slides.sub: Everyone can write binary search, almost nobody bug-free
slides.main: Test on arrays of zero, one and two elements — that's where all bugs live.

captions: Decide in advance whether bounds are inclusive and write the loop condition to match
Middle via half the difference — safer with fixed-width integers
Move past the middle — a checked element is never examined again
Typical bug: lo = mid; test arrays of 0, 1, 2 elements

frames.text: range [lo, hi): hi excluded; while lo < hi
lo = mid  → with hi = lo + 1 the loop never ends

slides.title: Lower and upper bounds
slides.sub: Find not a value but a place
slides.main: Found an equal element? Don't stop: shrink the range to the first suitable one.

captions: Lower bound — first element not less than the target (2): index 1
Upper bound — first element greater than the target: index 4
Difference of bounds = how many times the value occurs; lower bound = where to insert

slides.title: Binary search on the answer
slides.sub: Search not an array but the space of possible answers
slides.main: If you can ask a yes/no question about the answer and answers are monotonic, search binary.

captions: Not over an array but over answers: "does length L work?" — a linear check
If L works, every smaller one does too — answers T…T F…F
Binary search over length: check the middle and discard half the answers
The maximum valid length found in log(range) checks

frames.text: T T T T T F F F

slides.title: Three elementary sorts
slides.sub: All quadratic, each with its own character
slides.main: The secret of insertion sort: nearly linear on almost sorted data.

captions: Array 5, 2, 4, 1, 3 — three quadratic sorts
Bubble: each pass floats the maximum to the end
Selection: the minimum goes to the first spot of the unsorted part — few swaps
Insertion: each new element slides left into place — fast on almost sorted data

slides.title: Stability
slides.sub: A question that comes up in every interview
slides.main: Stability is a tool, not a detail: use it deliberately.

captions: Records with key and tag: keys 2, 1, 2, 1
Stable: equal keys kept their original order (b before d, a before c)
Unstable: the order of equals is shuffled

frames.text: b → d, a → c: order kept ✓
d → b, c → a: order lost ✗

slides.title: Quicksort
slides.main: A pivot, one linear pass, recursion — and the array is sorted.

captions: Pick a pivot (6) and split the rest in one pass
Smaller go left, larger go right; the pivot is in its final place
The same scheme recursively for the left part: pivot 3
All in place, O(1) memory (ignoring the stack), n log n on average

slides.title: The queen's dark side
slides.main: Quicksort's quadratic case is not a hypothesis but a constructible one.

captions: Pivot near the median: logarithmic depth, n log n total
Pivot always an extreme (sorted data): each part is "one lonely element and the rest": depth n, total n²
Random pivot, median of three, introspective switch to heap

slides.title: Merge sort
slides.main: No bad data at all: guaranteed n log n and stability.

captions: Split in half recursively — down to single elements
Merge sorted parts: two pointers, the smaller head goes first
Guaranteed n log n, stable; the price is O(n) extra memory

slides.title: Merging beats merge sort
slides.sub: Two sorted streams into one in linear time
slides.main: Merging two sorted lists is needed in dozens of places.

captions: Merge two sorted lists in linear time
Logs of two services by time — the same operation
Data too big for memory: sort chunks, write to disk, merge into big runs
Intersecting two sorted lists — a related scheme

slides.title: Heap
slides.sub: A tree hidden inside an array
slides.main: No bad data at all: the worst case equals the average.

captions: A heap in an array: the largest at the top
Swap the top with the last element — 9 is in place
Sift the new top down; the heap is one shorter
n times log n: O(n log n) worst case, O(1) memory

slides.title: What libraries use
slides.main: The best traits of different sorts combined in one.

captions: Timsort finds ordered runs, sorts small pieces by insertion and merges: nearly O(n) on partly ordered data
Introsort: quicksort by default, heap when deep, insertion on small pieces
There is no best sort in general — there's one that fits your data

slides.title: Today's practice
slides.main: A pattern settles in your head only through your hands.

captions: Binary search with a lower bound — test on duplicates
Insertion sort on almost sorted data — the result will surprise you
Two stable sorts give a sort by two keys
A sawmill problem will cement binary search on the answer

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Stability is a tool, not a detail: use it deliberately.

captions: Linear for unordered data, binary for ordered
Bounds beat exact hits; search on the answer cuts brute force to a logarithm
Insertion, quick, merge, heap: each has its strength
Use stability deliberately
